changes.before: If select becomes reject, which mapped array is printed?
changes.after: Select keeps items that pass a test. Map then makes a new result from each item kept.

before:
Enumerable supplies iteration helpers to classes with each. map builds results from each block return; select keeps original elements with truthy block results; reject keeps those whose block results are false or nil.

reject receives a block and returns a new array of the original elements for which that block is false or nil. The source array stays unchanged.
```ruby
values = [1, 2, 3, 4]
p values.reject { |n| n.even? }
p values
```
It prints:
```text
[1, 3]
[1, 2, 3, 4]
```
These non-bang array operations return new arrays rather than replacing the receiver. even? tests integer parity; p prints an inspected array with brackets, making its shape visible.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
values = [1, 2, 3, 4]
p values.select { |n| n.even? }.map { |n| n * 10 }
p values

```

Expected output or behavior: [20, 40]
[1, 2, 3, 4]. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare map with select when the block returns numbers, remembering that zero is truthy. You may trace it without a Ruby interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: Select keeps items that pass a test. Map then makes a new result from each item kept.
Only two and four go on to the multiplication.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```ruby
values = [1, 2, 3, 4]
p values.select { |n| n.even? }.map { |n| n * 10 }
p values
```
The output is `[20, 40]`, then `[1, 2, 3, 4]`. The new list holds twenty and forty. The original list is printed unchanged.
Replace select with reject to reverse which items stay.
